title: Longest Shared-Factor Chain
source: Pattern reported by an Infosys SP candidate (LeetCode Discuss, March 2025: online-test problems tagged 'DP + GCD' and 'DP + HashMap + Prime Factorization (Hard)') - the exact statement was not published; this is an original problem built on that pattern
statement:
You are given an array `A` of `N` positive integers.

Choose a subsequence `B[1], B[2], …, B[m]` (keep the original order, delete any elements) such that every two **consecutive** chosen elements share a common factor greater than `1`:

`gcd(B[j], B[j+1]) > 1` for all `1 ≤ j < m`.

A single element is always a valid chain (even `1`). Print the maximum possible length `m`.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `N`.
The second line contains `N` space-separated integers `A[1..N]`.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the length of the longest chain.

samples.explanation: For example `21 → 15 → 35` (`gcd = 3`, then `5`) or `10 → 15 → 35`. No chain of length 4 exists.
No two elements share a factor greater than 1.

hints: The `O(N^2)` LIS-style DP (`dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j]` with `gcd(A[j], A[i]) > 1`) is correct but needs `5·10^9` gcd calls for `N = 10^5`.
`gcd(x, y) > 1` ⇔ `x` and `y` have a **common prime factor**. A number `≤ 10^5` has at most 6 distinct prime factors.

Keep `best[p]` = longest chain found so far whose last element is divisible by prime `p`. For each `x` with distinct primes `P(x)`: `cur = 1 + max(best[p] for p in P(x))`, then set `best[p] = max(best[p], cur)` for every `p` in `P(x)`. Factorise quickly with a smallest-prime-factor sieve.
editorial:
### Reformulate the condition
`gcd(x, y) > 1` exactly when some prime `p` divides both. So the previous element of the chain only matters through **which primes divide it**.

### State
`best[p]` = maximum length of a valid chain among the elements processed so far whose **last element is divisible by `p`**.

### Transition (scan left to right)
For element `x` with distinct prime factors `P(x)`:
- `cur = 1 + max(best[p] for p in P(x))` (or `1` if `x = 1`, which has no primes)
- for every `p` in `P(x)`: `best[p] = max(best[p], cur)`

Compute **all** reads before any writes for the same `x` (otherwise `x` could chain to itself).

### Factorisation
A smallest-prime-factor sieve up to `max(A)` lets you factor each number in `O(log x)`.

### Complexity
Sieve `O(M log log M)`, DP `O(N · 6)`. Answer = max `cur` seen.

### Common mistakes
- Using the `O(N^2)` gcd DP - TLE.
- Iterating over all divisors instead of prime divisors (more work, same answer).
- Updating `best[p]` while still reading other primes of the same `x`.
- Forgetting that `1` forms a chain of length 1 but can never be linked to anything.
